[SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, sorry, doctor, I know I'm a few minutes behind. The fourteen was held up at the junction by the market, you know how it gets on a Thursday, and I thought, if I am driving it myself I would have gone round by the canal road.

[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Something on the sock.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): A, a stain. Yellowish. It's fine, I put a plaster on it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, right.

[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Both feet, a bit. They have been tingling and sort of dead, like when you sit wrongly, for about a week now. Maybe a bit more than a week. I thought it was the pedals.

[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Now you say it, I have been feeling a bit feverish. Hot and cold in the evenings. Not all the time. Two weeks I'd say, about two weeks, off and on.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. And you didn't think to mention it.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I thought it was the flu going round. Half the depot has it.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has anyone, you or your wife, looked at the foot properly in the light?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Um, she did, on Sunday. She said some things in Marathi that I will not repeat.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough, I'd have said something too. Any confusion, being muddled, or very sleepy?

[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, many years. Since my daughter was in school. Ten, twelve years.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what do you take for it?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformin. The white ones. Five hundred, two times in a day, morning and night with the food.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Five hundred twice a day, okay. Nurse, what do we have on the repeat?

[SEG0046] person_3 (NURSE): Well, um, it might be that they gave you the five hundred with two tablets? Some people take two.

[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right. I'm not going to argue about it right now, we'll sort out what the correct dose is, I'll get the pharmacy to confirm what they've been giving you. What else?

[SEG0076] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm-hm.
[SEG0077] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. The sock is a bit stuck.
[SEG0078] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, careful, careful, let me. Oh. Yes.
[SEG0079] person_3 (NURSE): Oh dear. Doctor, that's, can I get the dressing tray?
[SEG0080] person_2 (DOCTOR): Please. Mr Deshmukh, that isn't a blister. Can you feel me pressing here?
[SEG0081] person_1 (PATIENT): Where?
[SEG0082] person_2 (DOCTOR): Here, on your ankle.
[SEG0083] person_1 (PATIENT): Slightly. A bit. Not much. Is it bad?
[SEG0084] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me finish looking. The pulses at the ankle are weak but I can feel them. There's an ulcer on the ball of your right foot, about two centimetres across, and the skin round it is red and warm and swollen. There's some discharge on the old plaster.
[SEG0085] person_1 (PATIENT): Two centimetres, that's like a coin.
[SEG0086] person_2 (DOCTOR): Roughly, yes. A smaller coin.
[SEG0087] person_1 (PATIENT): But it doesn't hurt.
[SEG0088] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's the diabetes. The nerves in your feet don't tell you when something is wrong, which is why the numbness and why you can drive eight hours on it. The skin breaks down underneath you and you don't know.
[SEG0089] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm.
[SEG0090] person_2 (DOCTOR): It looks infected to me. With the fever and the redness, and you being diabetic, that's what I think we're dealing with, an infected diabetic foot ulcer. The pressure from the shoe and from the pedals has probably made it worse, or started it, so some of it may simply be damage from the pressure, but the fever says infection.
[SEG0091] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, so what do I do, tell me, madam. I have the late shift tomorrow.
[SEG0092] person_2 (DOCTOR): You won't be driving tomorrow, I'm sorry. I'll write you off for now.
[SEG0093] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah, but the roster.
[SEG0094] person_2 (DOCTOR): The roster will manage. I want to do some blood tests today, to see how high the infection is and to check your sugar and your kidneys, because that matters for the antibiotic. And the nurse will take a swab from the ulcer, so we know what's growing.
[SEG0095] person_3 (NURSE): Right.
[SEG0096] person_3 (NURSE): I'll do the swab after I clean it, Mr Deshmukh, it won't hurt, you'll hardly feel it.
[SEG0097] person_1 (PATIENT): That I believe.
[SEG0098] person_2 (DOCTOR): And I'm going to start you on an antibiotic today without waiting for the swab, it's called amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, six hundred and twenty-five milligrams, three times a day for seven days, with food.
[SEG0099] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay.
[SEG0100] person_1 (PATIENT): Three times, with food, fine.
[SEG0101] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the swab shows something different we'll change it. Keep the foot dry, keep the dressing on, don't walk around barefoot even at home. And no new shoes, wear the old ones, or sandals with a strap.
[SEG0102] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm-hm.
[SEG0103] person_1 (PATIENT): The old ones are worse.
[SEG0104] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we'll talk to the foot clinic about proper insoles. Now listen carefully. If the redness starts to creep up the foot, or up the leg, or if the fever gets worse, or you start feeling unwell, shivering, confused, you come in the same day, don't wait for your wife to ring me.
[SEG0105] person_1 (PATIENT): She will ring you anyway.
[SEG0106] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. I'd like to see you in the clinic in two days for the dressing, either way. Do you have any questions?
[SEG0107] person_1 (PATIENT): One, only one. Will they cut it? The foot? My cousin in Nashik lost two toes.
[SEG0108] person_2 (DOCTOR): I can't promise anything today, and I won't pretend it's nothing, but we've caught it at a stage where tablets and dressings should be enough. That's the plan, anyway. Which is why I'm cross that nobody saw it for weeks.
[SEG0109] person_1 (PATIENT): I know. I know. I will tell her she was right.
[SEG0110] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can tell her from me as well. Nurse, can we get him booked in for Saturday morning, I'm in until noon?
[SEG0111] person_3 (NURSE): I'll put him down for ten. Mr Deshmukh, come with me, and we'll do the blood now and then the dressing, and I'll give you the leaflet with the numbers.
[SEG0112] person_1 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. Thank you. And sorry again for being late.
[SEG0113] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're not late, you're early. By about three weeks.
